lead: A wire rope is a bundle of steel wires twisted into strands and then into a rope. It carries load only in tension: every wire shares the pull, so the rope is strong yet bends round a sheave. Cranes, lifts, mine hoists and bridge stays use it where a chain would be too heavy or a belt would slip. Selection fixes the construction and lay, sizes the diameter from the breaking load, and then checks the factor of safety once the bending over the sheave and the starting acceleration are counted.
prereq: You need: the place of rope among flexible drives from flexible drives and belt materials, and direct stress and the factor of safety from the design foundations.

blocks.text: The first number in 6×19 is the number of strands; the second is the number of wires in each strand. A standard 6×19 strand has 12 outer wires, 6 inner wires and 1 centre wire. Many small wires give flexibility, while the total steel area gives strength. A fibre core of sisal, manila or polypropylene holds lubricant and keeps the rope round. An independent wire rope core, written IWRC, is itself a small rope; it adds strength and resists crushing on the drum and heat.

blocks.text: Ropes such as 6×61 go further for very severe bending. Spiral strand rope has layers of wires round a centre with no separate strands; locked coil rope has shaped outer wires that interlock into a smooth, closed surface. Both are for standing duty such as bridge stays and guys, not for running over small sheaves.

In a regular lay, also called cross lay, wires in a strand run opposite to the direction of the strands around the rope. The rope is stable: a free load does not spin much. Right-hand regular lay is the usual default. In a lang lay, wires and strands run the same way. Lang lay is more flexible and puts more wire length on the sheave, so it wears longer, but it tends to untwist under load. Use it only with guided loads or fixed ends.

Right-hand and left-hand describe the helix of the strands. Hold the rope vertical: if the strands climb to the right like the thread of an ordinary screw, the lay is right-hand. Lay length is the length of rope in which one strand makes one full turn, about six to seven rope diameters in ordinary ropes. The lay direction is matched to the drum grooving so that winding does not unlay the rope, so state both lay type and direction when ordering.

For a single-fall lift, choose regular lay. For a scraper rope or a rope with both ends fixed, lang lay can be considered. A free load on lang lay will rotate, which twists the falls and can damage the rope.

A hoist rope carries more than the payload. The pull at the top of the rope is the load W plus the rope’s own weight wl (w in N/m, l the hanging length in m), and while the load speeds up at a m/s² both are multiplied by (1 + a/g). A rope that is slack when the drive starts takes an impact on top of this, so hoists are started with the rope taut.

blocks.where: F<sub>t</sub> is the largest steady pull in the rope in N; g = 9.81 m/s². The direct stress is σ<sub>t</sub> = F<sub>t</sub>/A, where A is the metallic area, about 0.4d² for 6×19 (d in mm, A in mm²).

blocks.text: σb = Er dw / D, where σb is the bending stress in the outer wires in N/mm²; Er is the modulus of the rope, about 0.8 × 10⁵ N/mm² for steel ropes, lower than the 2.1 × 10⁵ N/mm² of the wire because the wires lie in helices; dw is the outer wire diameter, about d/15 for 6×19; D is the sheave or drum diameter in mm. Multiplying by the area gives the equivalent bending load Fb = σbA.

n = (Fu − Fb) / Ft, where n is the factor of safety with bending counted; Fu is the breaking load of the rope (from the maker’s table, or σuA with σu the ultimate stress on the metallic area). Required values run from about 5 for a plain hoist to well above 10 for fast passenger lifts; the code for the machine sets the figure.

items: Fix the duty, the load W, the lift l and the starting acceleration a.
Choose the construction, core and lay.
Make a first estimate of d from F<sub>u</sub> = n × W with A = 0.4d², and round up to a standard size.
Check D/d against the smallest sheave for the construction.
Find F<sub>t</sub>, σ<sub>b</sub> and F<sub>b</sub>, then n = (F<sub>u</sub> − F<sub>b</sub>)/F<sub>t</sub>.
If n is too low, take the next rope size, a larger sheave or more falls.

blocks.text: In a block with n<sub>f</sub> supporting falls and overall efficiency η, the drum-side rope pull is W/(n<sub>f</sub>η), so more falls allow a thinner rope.

figure.caption: A 6×19 strand: twelve outer wires, six inner wires and one core wire around the fibre core at the rope centre. The outer wires take most of the bending when the rope runs over a sheave.

spec.aria: The layers of a 6×19 rope from the outer wires of a strand inward to the core, drawn as nested layers.

examples.question: A goods hoist lifts a cage and load of 1000 kg through 30 m and starts with an acceleration of 1 m/s². It uses a 6×19 fibre-core rope over a 500 mm sheave. The rope’s ultimate stress on its metallic area is 1400 N/mm², A = 0.4d², d<sub>w</sub> = d/15, E<sub>r</sub> = 0.8 × 10⁵ N/mm² and the rope weighs 0.45 kg/m. Take a first size from a factor of safety of 6 on the load alone, then find the factor of safety with the rope weight, the acceleration and the bending counted.
steps: Rope area and breaking load: A = 0.4 × 11² = 48.4 mm²; F<sub>u</sub> = 1400 × 48.4 = 67 760 N.
Sheave check: D/d = 500/11 = 45.5, above the 30d minimum for 6×19.
examples.answer: Adopt an 11 mm 6×19 rope (first estimate 10.25 mm). On the load alone its factor of safety is 67 760/9810 = 6.91; with the rope weight, starting acceleration and bending it falls to 5.67, which is acceptable for a goods hoist. A passenger lift would need a much higher factor and several ropes.
examples.check:
import math
W = 1000*9.81; su, k = 1400.0, 0.4
d0 = math.sqrt(6*W/su/k); d = 11.0
A = k*d*d; Fu = su*A
wl = 0.45*9.81*30; Ft = (W + wl)*(1 + 1/9.81)
sb = 0.8e5*(d/15)/500; Fb = sb*A
print(round(d0, 2), A, Fu, round(500/d, 1), round(wl, 1), round(Ft), round(Ft/A, 1), round(sb, 1), round(Fb), round((Fu - Fb)/Ft, 2))

traps: Stopping at the static factor of safety. In the worked example 67 760/9810 = 6.91 looks safe, but counting the rope weight, the starting acceleration and the bending load brings it to 5.67.
Reading 6×19 as 6 wires and 19 strands. It means 6 strands, with 19 wires in each strand.

Using the modulus of steel wire, 2.1 × 10⁵ N/mm², in σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D. The rope modulus, about 0.8 × 10⁵ N/mm², is the one used; the wire value would give 308 N/mm² instead of 117.3 N/mm² in the worked example.
Treating lang lay as the default for a free load. Lang lay is more flexible and wears longer, but it tends to untwist; regular lay is the stable default.
Mixing area definitions. A = 0.4d² for 6×19 is not the same as A = k(π/4)d²; in that second form k is about 0.51 for the same rope.

quiz.q: What does the designation 6×37 mean for a wire rope?
quiz.a: Six strands, with 37 wires in each strand.
An independent wire rope core: a small wire rope used as the core of a larger rope, giving higher strength and resistance to crushing.

quiz.q: Why does lang lay tend to untwist under load?
quiz.a: The wires and strands are twisted in the same direction, so the load produces a torque that tries to unwind the rope. Regular lay has opposite twists, which balance and keep the rope stable.

quiz.q: Why is the ratio D/d kept large when a rope runs over a sheave?
quiz.a: The bending stress in the outer wires is σ<sub>b</sub> = E<sub>r</sub>d<sub>w</sub>/D, so a larger sheave diameter D lowers it, raises the factor of safety and lengthens the fatigue life.

quiz.q: A 6×19 rope has diameter 12 mm, k = 0.4 and ultimate strength 1600 N/mm². Find its breaking load.
A 20 mm 6×19 rope runs over a 600 mm sheave. Take E<sub>r</sub> = 0.8 × 10⁵ N/mm² and d<sub>w</sub> = d/15. Find the bending stress.
A hoist uses 6×19 regular lay rope with D/d = 25. Suggest two changes and state the effect of each.
quiz.a: Increase the sheave diameter so that D/d reaches at least 30, the usual minimum for 6×19, which lowers the bending stress. Or change to a more flexible rope such as 6×37, whose finer wires (d<sub>w</sub> about d/22) accept sheaves down to about 18d.

quiz.q: Compare a fibre core and an IWRC for a hot, heavy mine hoist.
quiz.a: Fibre core holds lubricant and is flexible, but it is weaker and less resistant to heat and crushing. IWRC adds steel area, resists crushing and heat better, and suits heavy hot duties, at the cost of less flexibility and higher weight.

beyond: Not for the exam. In service, wire ropes fail by fatigue, wear and corrosion long before they reach ultimate strength. Inspectors use electromagnetic instruments and visual checks for broken wires, and discard criteria depend on the duty. Offshore moorings use spiral strand and locked coil ropes; elevators use compacted or 8×19 ropes. Search next for wire rope discard standards, rope fatigue testing and non-destructive evaluation of steel wire ropes.
